name: Liu Tsung-yüan
bio: Liu Tsung-yüan is a Chinese poet named in Charles Budd’s Chinese Poems (1912). Budd, who spells the name Liu Tsong-yuen, places him in the T’ang dynasty and gives no further note for him.
The poems here are Charles Budd’s versions in Chinese Poems (1912), given under the poet’s name as Budd romanises it.

poems.title: Midnight in the Garden
poems.author: Liu Tsung-yüan
poems.text:
The midnight hours were passing
  And sleep still past me flew;
My mind--so keenly working--
  Could hear the dropping dew.

So from my bed arising
  I open wide the door--
The western park revealing,
  And hills that heavenward soar.

Across the Eastern ranges
  The clear moon coldly shines
On bamboos, loosely scattered,
  And trailing mountain vines.

And so intense the stillness,
  That from the distant hills
I hear the pigeons cooing,
  And murmuring streams and rills.

For hours I have been thinking,
  As in a silent dream,
And now beyond the mountains
  I see the dawn's first gleam.

poems.title: River-Snow
poems.author: Liu Tsung-yüan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
A hundred mountains and no bird,
A thousand paths without a footprint;
A little boat, a bamboo cloak,
An old man fishing in the cold river-snow.

poems.title: From the City-Tower of Liu-chou
poems.author: Liu Tsung-yüan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
At this lofty tower where the town ends, wilderness begins;
And our longing has as far to go as the ocean or the sky . . .
Hibiscus-flowers by the moat heave in a sudden wind,
And vines along the wall are whipped with slanting rain.
Nothing to see for three hundred miles but a blur of woods and mountain —
And the river's nine loops, twisting in our bowels. . .
This is where they have sent us, this land of tattooed people —
And not even letters, to keep us in touch with home.

poems.title: Reading Buddhist Classics with Ch'ao at His Temple in the Early Morning
poems.author: Liu Tsung-yüan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
I clean my teeth in water drawn from a cold well;
And while I brush my clothes, I purify my mind;
Then, slowly turning pages in the Tree-Leaf Book,
I recite, along the path to the eastern shelter.
. . . The world has forgotten the true fountain of this teaching
And people enslave themselves to miracles and fables.
Under the given words I want the essential meaning,
I look for the simplest way to sow and reap my nature.
Here in the quiet of the priest's temple-courtyard,
Mosses add their climbing colour to the thick bamboo;
And now comes the sun, out of mist and fog,
And pines that seem to be new-bathed;
And everything is gone from me, speech goes, and reading,
Leaving the single unison.

poems.title: Dwelling by a Stream
poems.author: Liu Tsung-yüan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
I had so long been troubled by official hat and robe
That I am glad to be an exile here in this wild southland.
I am a neighbour now of planters and reapers.
I am a guest of the mountains and woods.
I plough in the morning, turning dewy grasses,
And at evening tie my fisher-boat, breaking the quiet stream.
Back and forth I go, scarcely meeting anyone,
And sing a long poem and gaze at the blue sky.

poems.title: An Old Fisherman
poems.author: Liu Tsung-yüan
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
